title: A hymn in Tilang
hookLine: Tilang holds Guru Nanak's hymn to Lalo about Babur's invasion, and its promise of a time for truth

lines: WHEN DO YOU SAY THE HARD THING?
cards: When is the right time to say a hard, true thing? Right away, while it's raw? Later, when it's safe?
Only to the people in charge? A page into the Tilang section, Guru Nanak gives his answer in the middle of a disaster. An army has come down from Kabul.
Wedding songs have turned into songs of blood. And the hymn is addressed to one man by name, again and again: Lalo. Today: a hymn in Tilang, and what it does with the truth.

teach.b: Earlier on this path you heard this shabad as courage, and as a word told first to a working man. Today, watch its moves. First, it names what went missing.
In paraphrase: modesty and dharma have both hidden themselves, and falsehood walks about as the leader. Before counting any damage, it says what vanished from public life: shame and right living.

teach.h: THE QAZIS AND BRAHMINS PUSHED ASIDE.
teach.b: Second, who was pushed aside: the qazis and the brahmins, the religious officials of both communities, have lost their place.

teach.h: GRIEF ON EVERY SIDE IS COUNTED.
teach.b: Third, who suffered, and it doesn't stop at one side. The Muslim women read their scripture and in their pain cry out to Khuda, God. Women of the Hindu castes, high and low, are counted in the same reckoning.
Yesterday Tilang spoke in the words of Muslim neighbors; here, in the same raga, grief crosses the same line. Nobody's suffering is left out to make a point. Fourth, when.

teach.h: TRUTH AT THE TIME OF TRUTH.
teach.b: Near its close, on the next page, Guru Nanak says he speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time of truth. That's the answer to the hook's question.
Not when it's comfortable, and not only when someone powerful asks. When it's true, and the time has come.
That's truth to power: the power never gets a vote on the timing. Whatever followed, the shabad was sung, kept and set in the Granth, where it is still sung in Tilang.

how: Guru Nanak's Tilang hymn addressed to Bhai Lalo is sung in kirtan in Raga Tilang, and its line about speaking as the Master's word comes is quoted by some Sikhs as a standard for honest speech.

games.q: what does “a hymn in tilang” mean?
o: Guru Nanak's hymn to Lalo, telling the truth at its time
a lullaby sung for Lalo's children in his town
a hymn praising the army that came down from Kabul

games.q: inside the Tilang hymn — tap the pairs.
p: when Nanak will tell the truth

s: the hymn mourns only one community
it names Muslim women crying out to Khuda and Hindu women of high and low castes alike.
the hymn is addressed to Lalo by name
Lalo's name returns at the end of its lines.
the hymn says to wait until truth is safe to tell
it says Nanak will tell the truth at the time of truth.

games.q: you've seen an invasion up close. the powerful are rising, and you have a song. what do you do with it?
o: keep quiet until things settle down.
sing what you saw, plainly, to a friend by name.
sing it only to the new rulers, carefully.
games.why: Guru Nanak sings it to Lalo, naming what vanished, who was pushed aside and who suffered, and says he'll tell the truth at the time of truth.

practice: If you'd like, listen to this hymn, often searched as jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee, or let one true thing come to mind that you haven't said yet; it might be small.
Shape it into one plain sentence, without blame and without softening, and simply hold it, with no need to say it today, and with one Waheguru if you pray.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Tilang. Guru Nanak's song to Lalo about the invasion: what vanished, who was pushed aside, who grieved, and truth told at the time of truth. Today's word.

orig.note: lalo, remembered by tradition as a carpenter of Saidpur, the friend this Tilang hymn is addressed to.

carryVoice: Your line: truth to power. Truth at the time of truth, kind as well as true. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Tilang Mahalla 1, Ang 722–723 (jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee; modesty and dharma hidden, falsehood leading; qazis and brahmins displaced; Muslim and Hindu women suffering; truth at the time of truth)
Guru Nanak and Bhai Lalo at Saidpur
